journeys.title: Find your way around
journeys.goal: See what the GUI is made of before changing anything in it.

steps.narrative: The sidebar on the left lists your notebooks. Help is one of them: the documentation is seeded into your library as ordinary read-only notes, so you can search it alongside everything else.

postcondition.narrative: the Help notebook is present in the sidebar

journeys.title: Write a note, and read it back
journeys.goal: Create a note and get something into it.

steps.narrative: Click New note. The note is created immediately and opens for editing; there is no dialog to fill in first.
Type into the editor. What you write is Markdown, and the preview beside it renders as you go.

postcondition.narrative: the editor is open with the note in it

journeys.title: Choose which notebook a note goes in
journeys.goal: File a note somewhere other than where it landed.

steps.narrative: Start from a new note.
Open the notebook picker. It sits with the note rather than in a menu, because which notebook a note belongs to is part of the note.

postcondition.narrative: the notebook picker is open and offering somewhere to file the note

journeys.title: Tag a note
journeys.goal: Put a tag on the note you are writing, and take one off.

steps.narrative: Start from a note. Tags belong to a note, so there has to be one open.

Open the tag control. It sits in the editor toolbar beside the notebook control, because both answer where this note belongs and both belong where you are typing. The label shows how many tags the note carries.
Type the tag. Tags are hierarchical, so `field/dusk` sits under `field`. Press Enter or use Add.
Add it. Each tag then appears as a chip with its own remove button, rather than as a comma-separated line you have to edit carefully.

postcondition.narrative: the tag control is showing the note's tags

journeys.title: Change a note you already wrote
journeys.goal: Open an existing note, change it, and save the change.

steps.narrative: All notes is every note in the library, whichever notebook it is filed in. Start here when you know what a note is called but not where you put it.
Click a note in the results list to open it. The editor fills with the note as it stands; nothing is changed by opening it.
The title is an ordinary field at the top of the editor. Change it the way you would change any text.
Saving writes a new revision rather than overwriting the old one, so the version you just replaced is still there.

postcondition.narrative: the note is open with its new title, saved as a fresh revision

journeys.title: Delete a note
journeys.goal: Move a note to the Trash and confirm it arrived there.

steps.narrative: Find the note first. Deleting is something you do to an open note, not to a row in a list, so that it is always clear which note is about to go.
Open the note you mean to delete and read it once. This is the last screen on which its text is in front of you.

Deleting asks you to confirm, and names the note it is about to move so that a mis-clicked row cannot become a deleted note. Deleting moves it to the Trash; it is not destroyed, and nothing here empties the Trash on a timer.
Trash is a place you can open and look inside, not a countdown. The note is in it.

postcondition.narrative: the deleted note is listed in the Trash

journeys.title: Take a note back out of the Trash
journeys.goal: Restore a deleted note and confirm it is back among your notes.

steps.narrative: Open the Trash to see what is in it. Everything here was deleted and none of it is gone.
Open the note you want back. A trashed note opens read-only, with a badge saying why.
Restoring returns the note to the notebook it was filed in, not to some general inbox.
All notes again, to see it where it belongs.

postcondition.narrative: the restored note is listed among the notes again

journeys.title: Search for a note
journeys.goal: Find notes by what they say, using the same query language the command line takes.

steps.narrative: The search box takes the query language, not just a word. Bare words are combined with an implicit AND; an uppercase OR widens the search instead.
Run the search. Results are ordered by relevance and page as you scroll, so a large library does not have to be loaded to be searched.

postcondition.narrative: notes matching either side of the OR are listed

journeys.title: Narrow a search by tag, and exclude what you do not want
journeys.goal: Use a field query and a negation together, which is what most real searches turn out to be.

steps.narrative: tag: matches a tag rather than the note's text, and a leading minus excludes. Here that is everything tagged field/dusk except the documentation.
The same box runs it. Every query-language feature works here exactly as it does in notriosctl search, because it is the same parser.

postcondition.narrative: only the tagged note outside the Help notebook is listed

journeys.title: Keep a search as a notebook
journeys.goal: Turn a search you have just watched work into a notebook in the sidebar.

steps.narrative: Search for whatever you want the notebook to hold. Any query works: this is the same language the rest of the interface takes.
Run it and read the results. This is the point of keeping a search here rather than typing one into a form: you are deciding about a query you have watched work, not one you hope is right.
Keep this search appears once a search has returned something. A query that found nothing is not offered, because a notebook made from it would open empty.
The query is suggested as the name and is usually not what you want to read in a sidebar. The query itself is shown below the field but cannot be edited here.
Keeping it adds a notebook to the sidebar whose contents are whatever the query matches, now and later.

postcondition.narrative: the kept search is listed in the sidebar as a notebook
